descriptionChirho: Financial profit or monetary gain derived from a business activity. In Acts 16:16,19 the slave girl with a spirit of divination brought her owners much profit (ergasian) through fortune-telling, and when the spirit was cast out their hope of profit (ergasias) was gone. Also in Acts 19:24 Demetrius the silversmith provided considerable business/profit (ergasian) to the craftsmen through making silver shrines. Cross-linguistically: Arabic ribhan (profit/gain), Hebrew revach/rivham (profit/their profit), Hindi kamai (earnings), Korean suigeul (profit/revenue), Spanish ganancia (gain), French travail (work, though context specifies monetary gain). The financial connotation is confirmed by the commercial narrative context in all three occurrences.

The active doing or practice of something, the carrying out of an activity. In Eph 4:19 those who have given themselves over to sensuality 'for the working of' (eis ergasian) every kind of impurity, where ergasia denotes the active practice or pursuit of sin. Cross-linguistically: Arabic amali (work/doing), Hebrew asiyat (the doing of), Hindi kaam (work/deed), Korean il-eul (work), Spanish practica (practice), French travail (work). This sense emphasizes the process of doing rather than any financial result, distinguishing it from the profit sense.

Earnest effort or diligence applied toward achieving something. In Luke 12:58 Jesus advises giving effort/diligence (dos ergasian) to settle with an adversary on the way to court, meaning 'make every effort' or 'do your utmost.' Cross-linguistically: Arabic juhdan (effort/exertion), Hebrew avodah (work/labor), Hindi koshish (effort/attempt), Korean sugoreul (labor/toil), Spanish esfuerzo (effort), French travail (work). The emphasis is on exertion and diligence rather than financial gain or mere activity, though the root meaning of 'work' underlies all three senses.

A business enterprise, trade, or craft as an ongoing occupation. In Acts 19:25 Demetrius gathers those engaged in the same trade/business (ergasias), referring to the silversmithing profession as a whole. Cross-linguistically: Arabic as-sinaati (the craft/trade), Hebrew avodah (work/occupation), Hindi vyapar (trade/business), Korean jig-eob (occupation/profession), Spanish negocio (business), French travail (work). This differs from the 'profit' sense (Acts 19:24) in that here ergasia denotes the trade itself rather than its financial yield, a distinction confirmed by Arabic sinaati (craft) vs. ribhan (profit) in the same chapter.
